subtitle.english: Our ships run a great risk

latin: Caesar naves longas<sup>1</sup> aedificari in flumine Ligere quod influit in Oceanum, remiges<sup>2</sup> ex provincia<sup>3</sup> institui, nautas gubernatoresque comparari<sup>4</sup> jubet...
Namque hostium naves ad hunc modum factae armataeque erant:
Carinae aliquanto planiores quam nostrarum navium, quo facilius vada<sup>5</sup> ac decessum aestus<sup>6</sup> excipere possent*;
Prorae admodum erectae atque item puppes ad magnitudinem fluctuum<sup>7</sup> tempestatumque accommodatae;
naves totae factae ex robore ad quamvis vim et contumeliam<sup>8</sup> perferendam*;
transtra<sup>9</sup> ex pedalibus in altitudinem trabibus<sup>10</sup> confixa clavis ferreis digiti pollicis crassitudine<sup>11</sup>;
ancorae, pro funibus, ferreis catenis revinctae<sup>12</sup>;
pelles pro velis... sive propter lini inopiam<sup>13</sup>, sive eo (quod est magis veri simile),
quod tantas tempestates oceani, tantosque impetus ventorum sustineri ac tanta onera navium regi velis non satis commode posse* arbitrabantur.
Nostra classis una celeritate et pulsu remorum praestabat;
reliqua, pro loci natura, pro vi tempestatum, illis erant aptiora et accommodatiora.

Neque enim his nostrae rostro<sup>14</sup> nocere poterant*, tanta in iis erat firmitudo, neque propter altitudinem facile telum adigebatur, et eadem de causa minus commode copulis<sup>15</sup> continebantur.
Tempestates facilius ferebant* et in vadis consistebant tutius<sup>16</sup> et ab aestu relictae nihil saxa et cotes<sup>17</sup> timebant;
quarum rerum omnium nostris navibus casus erat extimescendus<sup>18</sup>.
english: Caesar [orders that] warships (long [ships]) be built on the Loire, a river which flows into the Ocean, [that] rowers [come] from the province (be formed); [that] sailors and pilots be procured...
And [this is how] (for in this way) the ships of the enemies were built and armed:
The hulls [were] somewhat flatter than [those] of our ships, so that they could more easily [take] (support) the shallows and the [ebb] (going away) of the tide (see N. 5);
the prows [were] very raised, and likewise the poops, [to be] adapted to the size of the waves and of the storms;
the ships were entirely made [of] oak, to [be able to] take any violence and [any] blow;
the frames [were made] of beams a foot thick, fixed with iron nails [of] the thickness of the thumb (finger);
the anchors [were] moored by iron chains instead of ropes (pro funibus);
skins as sails... either because of the lack of linen, or because (eo + 2nd quod in P. 9) (which is more likely),

they thought (arbitrabantur) that the [so strong] storms of the Ocean, and the [so] violent assaults of the winds could not be withstood, and that [such] heavy ships could not be steered with [canvas] sails [easily enough] (satis commode).
Our fleet was superior [only] in speed and in the thrust of the oars;
[the rest], by reason of [local conditions] (nature of the place), [and] by reason of the force of the storms, [was to their advantage] (were for them more adapted and better suited).

Indeed, our [ships] could not harm theirs with their ram, so strong were they, nor, because of their height, [did] the missiles [easily reach] (were driven) [their aim]; and for this same reason they were [less easily held] with grappling hooks.
They bore storms more easily, they [stopped] with greater safety on the shallows, and, left [dry] by the tide, they did not fear rocks and reefs;
the risk of all these things was to be feared for our ships.

footnotes: Navis longa, warship, longer than a merchant ship (cf. navis oneraria, L. 10, P. 8).
Remex, -igis, m., rower; remus, -i, m., the oar.

Provincia, -ae, f., the Roman Province, which included Provence (to which it gave its name) and Languedoc, where its capital was (Narbo, -onis, m., Narbonne; the adjective Narbonensis, -e, designated this province, also called Narbonensis).

Comparare, to procure (parare = to prepare, cf. L. 27, N. 14); to compare is rather said conferre or componere (to carry or to put with); finally there exists another verb comparare (which comes from par, paris, equal, similar) which means: to assemble, to confront.

Vadum, -i, n., ford, or shallow (that is to say a place where, the bottom being high, the water is not very deep). Quo = ut eo, so that by this [means], is ordinarily followed by the comparative (here facilius).

Aestus, -us, m., here the tide; more generally the boiling due to heat (aestuare, to be very hot, to sweat great drops). At high tide, pleno aestu; at low tide, aestu recessu; decessus, -us, m., the ebbing tide, the ebb.
Fluctus, -us, m., the wave, the swell; not to be confused with fluxus, -us, m., the current, the flow. — Prora, -ae, f., prow (front of a vessel); puppis, -is, f., poop (rear of a vessel).
Transtrum, -i, n., crossbeam; here transverse members («frames») on which were fixed the longitudinal planks that formed the «planking» of the hull.

Trabs, trabis, f., beam. — Pedalis, -is, -e, (a foot) wide (or long); bipedalis (2 feet); sesquipedalis (1 foot 1/2, cf. L. 58, N. 7); verba sesquipedalia, words that go on and on. — Altitudo, -inis, f., is the third dimension (that is to say the height as well as the depth). E.g.: altitudo arboris, fossae, nivis: the height of a tree, the depth of a hole, the thickness of the snow (do you remember the two other dimensions: longitudo and latitudo?).

Pollex, -icis, m., the thumb (uncertain kinship with polleo, -es, -ere, to be strong); but an inch, a measure of length, is said digitus, -i, m., that is to say finger, and it is then a question of the Roman inch of 1/16 of a foot, whereas uncia (L. 60, N. 3), like the French pouce and the English inch, is 1/12. — Crassitudo, thickness; crassus, -a, -um, thick.

(Re)vincio, -is, -ire, vinxi, vinctum, to bind, to attach, to chain; vinculum, -i, n., the bond, the prisoner's chain; not to be confused with vinco, -is, -ere, vici, victum (cf. Caesar's veni, vidi, vici, I came, I saw, I conquered). There also exists another verb comparare (which comes from... no). Catena, -ae, chain (cf. French caténaire and cadenas). Funis, -is, m., the rope (cf. funicular).

Linum, -i, n., linen. — Inopia, -ae, f., the lack, comes from inops, -opis, adj., without resources (opes, opum, f. pl.). — Pro: prep. + abl.: in front of, or (here) in place of; signifies only in a few particular cases, pro Archia, the bond, the [speech] for Archias, that is to say pronounced by Cicero in the defence of Archias (cf. prout in the exercise, P. 5).
Rostrum, -i, n., the beak of a bird or the ram of a boat.
Copula, -ae, f., bond, link; here assured by means of a grappling hook; this word gave the French couple. — If you have not understood telum, refer to L. 86, N. 11.
Tutius, comparative of the adverb tute, in safety (from the adjective tutus, -a, -um, who is in safety).
Saxum, -i, n., rock. Cos, cotis, f., hard or cutting stone (stone for sharpening, whetstone); here, reef. One also finds cautes, -is, f., the reef.
Extimesco, -is, -ere, extimui (derived from timere, to fear) is an «inchoative» verb (cf. R. and N. 91) meaning to begin to fear.
comments: Cymba, -ae, f. (pr. kummba), light boat or bark. — Prout, or pro ut, conjunction, according as, in function of what... — Pando, -is, -ere, pandi, pansum, to spread. — Semel, once; bis, twice, ter, quater, quinquies, etc. — Subnecto, -is, -ere, nexui, nexum, to attach with a knot from below (necto, etc., to knot). In rigs of the old type, the surface of the sail is reduced (if the wind is too strong) by folding it partly on itself with the help of small cords called «reef points». In modern rigs, one rolls the bottom of the sail around a «roller boom». The command then becomes: Velum semel (bis, ter, etc.) circumvolvite!, take one (two, three, etc.) turns of the roller!

Note. — The end of the exercise, its translation, and the corresponding remarks are given to you as a curiosity. In fact we pose a problem rather than solve it. During the last five hundred years, the art of navigation (by sail or otherwise) has developed considerably, and has therefore required an increasingly precise vocabulary. As most nautical terms have been borrowed from the Nordic languages, the (provisional) lag taken by Latin is more difficult to make up than in the other domains, where it is only partial. If you have doubts about what we are advancing, it will be enough for you to consult modern Latin works, such as those of Descartes or of Newton, or even «ultra-modern» ones such as the De Physica Quantica of Soccorsi (1956, see Bibliographical Index), to realize that Latin is a living language particularly well suited to scientific communication.

We will not give you extracts from these texts, for they would interest only part of our readers. We simply hope that our little exercises without pretension will attract towards new studies those who wish to know more and thus to contribute to the progress of the Latin language.

latin: Potesne mihi auxilium ferre? Cymbarum certamini, quod hodie futurum est, interesse* cupio, sed collega egeo.
Consuetus enim mihi collega tertium diem aegrotat.
Sed artis nauticae ego non sum peritus!
Nihil timueris! Gubernabo ego et velum majus moderabor.
Tu autem velum anterius rudente prout te jussero contrahes aut laxabis.
Rudens quid est? — Est quod vulgus funem vocat, sed funem qui ad vela contrahenda vel laxanda usurpatur.
Scias oportet* instrumenta in navibus plurima esse, quae nauticarum rerum ignorantibus similia videntur, nomina tamen peculiaria habent.
Qua de causa nautae linguam vulgarem ita implicaverunt?
Quia verba quibus navarchus, quae nautis administranda sunt, imperat, brevia nec ambigua esse debent...
Ancoram solvite! Vela pandite! Velum majus semel artius subnectite! Gubernator! Vento quam maxime adverso cursum tene!
english: Can you do me a service? I would like to take part in [the regatta] (contest of small boats) which is to take place today, but I lack a crew member.
In fact, [my] usual crew member has been ill [for two days] (third day is ill).
But I am not [experienced] in [sailing] (the nautical art).
Don't fear anything! [It's] me [who] will steer and who will look after the [mainsail] (biggest sail).
You, [you will sheet] in or [ease] the jib (front sail) with the sheet according to what I [tell you] (will have ordered).
A sheet, what is that? — It's what [ordinary people] call a rope, but a rope that is only used to pull in or ease the sails.
You must know that in boats there are numerous instruments which, for people ignorant of the things of the sea, look similar, [but which] nevertheless have particular names.
For what reason have sailors complicated the [usual] (popular) language so much?
Because the words with which the captain commands the sailors what [they must] do, must be short and [unambiguous] (not ambiguous)...

Weigh anchor! [Hoist] (unfurl) the sails! [Take] a reef in the mainsail (once tighter fasten)! Helmsman! [Hold] the course [as close to the wind as possible] (the wind being the most adverse possible)!

sources.latin: E Bello Gallico, a Julio Caesare (III, 9... III, 13).
sources.english: (From the Gallic War by Julius Caesar (III, 9... III, 13).)
